name: Pure Blue
lede: Pure Blue is [[blue|Blue]] with no hint of green or violet pulling it either way, an intense, near-primary blue named by the modifier "pure" rather than by any pigment or place.

sections.title: The parent word plus a grammatical modifier
sections.body:
The name pairs the parent word [[blue|Blue]] with the modifier "pure", describing the hue itself (unmixed, with nothing added) rather than naming a dye, a mineral or a place; it was recorded in Randall Munroe's 2010 xkcd color-naming survey [1]. No earlier dictionary or plate in the books consulted here carries this exact phrase [1].

In printed English more generally, the phrase "pure blue" rose through the mid-1800s and peaked in the 1870s, a pattern that reflects the words' broader use (including non-color senses) and not this swatch specifically [2]. Its closest look-alikes on file are [[medium-blue|Medium Blue]], duller, and [[primary-blue|Primary Blue]], more vivid, two other entries from the same survey describing much the same near-primary blue, with [[zaffre|Zaffre]] a duller, darker match further out [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: No painting in our 23,781-painting archive carries a close match to this exact, highly saturated blue covering at least 1 percent of its canvas, as photographed [4]. That says something about the limits of our archive of historical paintings, not about painting in general: a blue this pure and intense, with almost no red or green mixed in, is rare in paint even where blue itself is common [4]. These are photographs of aged, varnished canvases, so the absence is a statement about this dataset, not a claim that the color never appears on canvas.
